idiom_name: #private-field composition + Symbol.dispose/using (WeakRef and FinalizationRegistry only as backstop)
implementation_notes: The whole is an object (or a closure) holding its parts in #private fields or captured variables, so parts are unreachable except through the whole's methods - the language gives encapsulation for free and no role classes are needed. Lifecycle is explicit: implement [Symbol.dispose]() (or close()) and let callers declare the whole with `using`/`await using`, which disposes in reverse declaration order when the scope exits and aggregates failures in SuppressedError; DisposableStack collects cleanups registered ad hoc. WeakRef and FinalizationRegistry cover the cases where a part, a cache or a listener must not keep the aggregation alive, but a conforming engine may never call a cleanup callback (notably at program shutdown), so they are backstops and never the release path.
pitfalls: Nothing warns you when the whole is declared with const or let instead of `using`, so disposal is skipped; only a linter or type checker can catch it.
`using` ties disposal to the block: a part (or the whole) still referenced after the block is an already-disposed resource, and dispose errors are wrapped in SuppressedError.
FinalizationRegistry callbacks must not close over the whole (that keeps it alive) and may run arbitrarily late or never, so handles can survive until process exit if you rely on them.
